Hook: In 1992 Christopher Sims ran the most careful vector autoregressions of the day, for five countries, asking what happens after a central bank raises its rate. We can repeat his American exercise with the data in our Data Room: industrial production, consumer prices and the federal funds rate, month by month from 1965 to 1995. Here is what consumer prices do after a one-point rise in the funds rate. They rise. For 36 months the price level is higher than it would have been, by up to 0.24 percent, and the band around the estimate does not include a fall for more than a year. Raising rates to fight inflation, it seems, raises inflation. It came to be called the price puzzle. Sims's own diagnosis was that the Federal Reserve raised rates when it saw inflation coming, using information the model did not have, so the model mistook the bank's foresight for the effect of its policy. Give the model a piece of what the bank saw, commodity prices, which move before consumer prices do, and the puzzle shrinks: after 22 months prices are lower, and after four years 1.1 percent lower. The data had not changed. The assumption had.

The question: with one history and no control group, how can anyone say what a policy did? What can a history of a few series say on its own? What assumptions turn its correlations into the effect of a policy? How are whole models of the economy estimated? And which answers survive, whatever the method?
Economics, Built. Part fifty-five: identifying macro.

By the end of this part you will be able to say what a vector autoregression identifies on its own, and what it cannot; five ways of identifying a shock, each tested on the Island's history, where the true effect of policy is known; how local projections and narrative and high-frequency instruments work; how a whole model of the economy is estimated, with the Kalman filter and the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, and what it cannot learn; and what regions, matched impulse responses and a few decades of argument have taught macroeconomics.
VAR: Chapter one. What a VAR knows, and what it does not.

In 1980 Christopher Sims proposed that macroeconomists stop imposing restrictions they could not defend. Let each variable, here output growth, inflation and the policy rate, depend on the recent past of all of them. That is a vector autoregression, and least squares estimates it equation by equation. What is left over each quarter, the surprises u, are mixtures of the shocks we care about, supply, demand and monetary policy, which nobody observes. Their covariance is B times B transposed. And here is the catch. With three variables the covariance of the surprises has six distinct numbers, but the mixing matrix B has nine. The data pin down six of them. Three must come from somewhere else.

Here is what that means on the Island. Fit a vector autoregression to 240 quarters of its history. Then take three different mixing matrices, each of which reproduces the covariance of the surprises exactly, and in each call one of the shocks monetary policy. Story one: a rise in the rate barely moves output or inflation. Story two: output edges up and inflation falls. Story three: output collapses and inflation jumps. All three fit the data equally well, to the last decimal. A vector autoregression summarizes a history; it does not, on its own, say what caused what. Every answer about the effect of policy comes from an assumption added to it, and the rest of this part is about which assumptions earn their place.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: which shock was it?

Your turn. The Island's economy is hit by three kinds of shock: a change in what it can produce, a change in what people want to spend, and a surprise from the central bank. Here is what each one does, unlabelled: output in blue, inflation in orange, the policy rate in pink, over three years. Which of A, B and C is a monetary tightening? Pause, and choose.

The answer is B. The rate jumps, and output and inflation fall: that is what a tightening should do. A is a demand shock, which pushes all three up together, and C is a supply shock, which raises output and lowers inflation. But notice how you knew. You did not read it off the data; you brought an expectation about what a tightening does, its signs, and matched it. That is an identifying assumption, and Harald Uhlig made it a method: sign restrictions, one of the five we turn to next.
Island: Chapter four. The five, on the Island's history.

On the Island we know the truth, so take one history of 240 quarters and try each scheme. In white, what a one-point rise in the rate truly does: output dips and recovers; inflation drops at once and fades. Timing gets it wrong. It forces the first-quarter effects to zero, which the Island's bank violates, so inflation barely moves and output falls less than it should. Signs give a band. For inflation it contains the truth for a year and a half; for output its middle runs well below it. The set of mixing matrices that obey the signs is wide, and how the band looks depends on how the candidates were drawn, as Christiane Baumeister and James Hamilton warned. The outside instrument lands near the truth, and so does the change in variance. One history is noisy, though; the instrument's output path wanders after two years.

So run each scheme on 300 histories and average. Timing is wrong on average, not by bad luck: inflation's first-quarter fall is minus 0.34 points, and timing says zero, by assumption, every time. The instrument and the change in variance are right on average, the variance a little noisier. And the long-run restriction answers a different question. It cannot separate demand from money, since neither moves output for ever, but it finds the supply shock: output up 1.26 percent for good, against 1.26 in truth. Each scheme is only as good as its assumption, and on the Island, unlike in the world, we can check.
Projections: Every scheme so far identified a shock and then let the fitted autoregression carry it forward, one quarter at a time. That chains the answer at two years to the model's every step in between. Òscar Jordà proposed asking each horizon directly: regress output h quarters ahead on today's shock, or its instrument, with controls, and read the response off the coefficient. One regression per horizon. Mikkel Plagborg-Møller and Christian Wolf showed that, in large samples and with enough lags, the two estimate exactly the same thing. In a real sample they differ in a familiar way: a short autoregression is biased but steady; a projection is nearly unbiased but noisy.

A race on the Island: 300 histories of 200 quarters, the effect of a one-point rise in the rate on output, every method using the same instrument. In white, the truth. In grey, an autoregression with one lag, when the Island's economy has two. Its band is tight, but at four years its average is off by 0.07: it carries its error forward. In blue, four lags: less bias, more spread. In gold, local projections: nearly unbiased, but by four years the band is twice as wide. Which to prefer depends on whether you fear bias or noise more. Dake Li, Plagborg-Møller and Wolf found the same trade-off across thousands of simulated economies: projections win on bias, autoregressions on variance.
Instruments: Chapter six. Narrative and high-frequency shocks.

The outside instrument did best on the Island. Where do good instruments come from in the world? Part thirty-one met two sources. Christina and David Romer read the Federal Reserve's own records and kept only the part of each decision that its staff's forecasts could not explain: the surprise, purged of foresight. Others look at the minutes around an announcement. The move in interest-rate futures in that window can only be news about policy, because nothing else happened. There is a catch. An announcement can also tell markets what the bank knows about the economy, so part of the surprise is news about the economy itself. Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson called it the information effect. Either series can be the outside instrument of Chapter three; Mark Gertler and Peter Karadi used market surprises that way in an autoregression.

Part thirty-one's Island reproduces the price puzzle on purpose: its bank sees news about coming cost shocks before it sets its rate. Averaged over 200 histories, the truth: inflation falls, slowly. A recursive autoregression says it rises, by up to 0.43 points: the puzzle, made by the bank's foresight. Give the model a noisy signal of the bank's news, as Sims gave his commodity prices, and the puzzle shrinks but does not vanish. Narrative shocks and clean market surprises both recover the truth. Surprises contaminated by an information effect understate it: part of what looks like policy is the bank's news about the economy. The cure for the price puzzle was never a cleverer regression. It was a better account of why the rate moved.
DSGE: Chapter seven. Estimating a DSGE model.

Autoregressions ask what the data say about one shock at a time. A dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model, a DSGE model, claims to account for everything at once, and can be estimated whole. Solve the model, here Part thirty's three equations with a demand shock, a cost shock and a monetary shock, and it becomes a state-space system: hidden states that evolve, and observed series that are combinations of them. The Kalman filter, from Part thirty-one, turns that into a likelihood: for any parameters, how probable the observed history is. Multiply by a prior, what we believed before, and Bayes's rule gives the posterior. To explore it, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm takes a random step, keeps it if the posterior is higher and sometimes even if it is lower, and repeats thousands of times. The places it visits are draws from the posterior. Sungbae An and Frank Schorfheide set out the recipe; Frank Smets and Rafael Wouters used it to estimate a model with seven observed series that central banks still build on.

The Island's version: 200 quarters of the output gap, inflation and the policy rate, generated by the model itself with parameters we chose. Here are the first thirty years. We estimate five parameters: the slope of the Phillips curve, the inverse of the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, the rule's response to inflation and to the output gap, and the persistence of policy shocks.

The results. For each parameter, the grey line is the prior, the gold bars the posterior, and the white line the truth. With all three series observed, every posterior is far narrower than its prior and sits near the truth: the Phillips curve's slope, for instance, is 0.106, with ninety percent of the posterior between 0.089 and 0.123, against a truth of 0.1. The data have taught us something about every parameter. That is not always so, as the next chapter shows.
Weak: Chapter eight. What the data cannot tell apart.

Now estimate the same model from the same history, but suppose the policy rate is not observed: only the output gap and inflation. The Phillips curve's slope is still learned, its posterior 21 percent as wide as the prior. But look at the other four. Their posteriors are 64 to 92 percent as wide as their priors, and centred near them. The answer looks like an estimate, with a mean and a band, but it is mostly the prior coming back out. Fabio Canova and Luca Sala showed that this happens in published models: some parameters barely move the likelihood, and a Bayesian posterior hides that unless it is compared with its prior.

Here is why. Fix sigma, re-estimate the other four, and record how well the model can then fit. With the rate observed, the fit falls off sharply on either side of the best value, by 35 log points by a sigma of three: sigma is pinned. Without the rate, the fit changes by only 1.5 log points across the whole range: almost any sigma can be made to fit by adjusting the others. When the likelihood is flat, the prior decides. The cure is not a cleverer sampler; it is data that move the parameter, here the rate itself.
Regions: Chapter nine. Macro from the cross-section.

One history is one data point. A cross-section has many. Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson compared American states that receive more or less of national military spending. Part thirty-two built such a union on the Island: 48 regions over 40 years, with one central bank. Compare regions within each year, and a region that gets a point more spending than average produces 1.53 points more output: the relative multiplier, planted at 1.5. But the nation's output rises only 0.56 per point of national spending, because the central bank leans against national spending, and cannot lean against one region's. Everything national, including monetary policy's response, is soaked up by the year effects that made the comparison clean. The regional estimate is right, and answers a different question. Christian Wolf showed how a model can bridge the two: the missing intercept is the price of using the cross-section.

The same logic powers the shift-share designs of Part thirty-six's China shock. A region's exposure is its mix of industries, times national shocks to those industries. Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, Isaac Sorkin and Henry Swift showed that such an instrument is valid if the industry shares are as good as random; Kirill Borusyak, Peter Hull and Xavier Jaravel, that it can instead be valid if the national shocks are, provided there are many of them. Either way, the answer compares regions with each other, and the effect on the nation as a whole has to come from somewhere else.
Matching: There is a middle way between estimating a whole model and estimating a single response. Lawrence Christiano, Martin Eichenbaum and Charles Evans first identified the effects of a monetary shock with an autoregression, then chose the parameters of a model to reproduce them. Estimate how the economy responds to the shock. Compute the same responses from the model, for any parameters. Weight each by how precisely it was measured, and minimize the distance: Part fifty-four's method of moments, with the responses as the moments.

On the Island: four hundred quarters of an economy like the one estimated in Chapter seven, but whose central bank surprises more often, and a market surprise as the instrument. The dots are the estimated responses of the output gap, inflation and the rate to a one-point surprise, with their standard errors. In grey, the model at a poor starting guess. In gold, the model after matching, with two parameters free: the curvature that governs how spending responds to the rate, and the slope of the Phillips curve. Sigma comes out at 1.48, against 1.5. The Phillips slope comes out at 0.072, against 0.1, and across sixty histories it ranges from 0.04 to 0.13: inflation's response is small and noisy, so the slope it implies is uncertain. The method can only be as sharp as the responses it matches.
Knows: Chapter eleven. Forecasts, and what macroeconomics knows.

If a model really knows what causes what, it should also forecast. Forecasting out of sample is the toughest test there is, because the model never saw the answer. The record at the turns is sobering. In August 2008 the professional forecasters expected the American economy to grow in 2009, by 1.5 percent; it shrank by 2.6 percent, more than in any year since 1946. In June 2021 the Federal Reserve's median projection had inflation falling to 2.1 percent in 2022; it was 6.1 percent. Models fitted to calm decades are least reliable at exactly the turning points that matter most. Part fifty-seven grades the forecasters, and the models, properly.

So what does macroeconomics know, and how does it know it? Valerie Ramey's survey of the shocks and their effects, and Nakamura and Steinsson's essay on identification, give a sober answer. Money is not neutral: a surprise tightening lowers output for a year or two and prices more slowly, and every credible method agrees on the sign and the delay. How much is contested: the estimates differ several times over with the method and the decades used, as the Dial will show. Regions are not the nation: relative multipliers are above one, national ones near or below it. And the clean findings, which Nakamura and Steinsson call identified moments, are the test a model must pass: not just matching averages, but reproducing what the best designs have found.
